newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nintendo says hard to raise 64-bit player output.
newsitem.headline: Nintendo says hard to raise 64-bit player output.

text.p: Japan's Nintendo Co Ltd said on Friday it will be difficult to raise production of its new 64-bit game players to meet booming demand in the United States.
"We were told the U.S. wants at least 1.5 million units of N64 by the Christmas season," spokesman Hiroshi Imanishi said.
"But it's not easy to boost our current production capacity of 500,000 units a month," he added.
Nintendo said on Wednesday that its entire 350,000-unit shipment of N64 video game players had sold out at U.S. retail stores just three days after their launch in late September.

The cutting-edge 64-bit game player, which improves the graphics and speed of its older 16-bit system, is crucial to Nintendo's bid to recapture the top spot in the hotly competitive $11 billion-a-year U.S. video game market.

Nintendo earlier this year set a U.S. price for the player of $250, betting consumers would pay more for the advanced player than for Sony's PlayStation and Sega's Saturn. But Nintendo later cut the price to $199.99 in line with similar machines from the two competitors.
Nintendo had planned to sell 600,000 units in the United States through the holiday season.

Imanishi said the company was trying to see if it was possible to increase shipments to the United States. But he declined to say whether it would be able to ship enough of the N64 products for the hot Christmas season.
He also said the strong demand in the United States would not translate into an immediate sharp improvement in Nintendo's business performance for the current year.
"We don't think the increased popularity in the United States would have a dramatic impact on our business performance for now," he said.
Nintendo also plans to launch the new game player in Europe in March 1997.
Nintendo launched the 64-bit game player in Japan early this summer after several postponements.
Some financial analysts say it appears that Japanese sales are slower than expected due to lack of attractive software, but Nintendo has denied this.
